newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba dismisses Clinton move on Helms-Burton.
newsitem.headline: Cuba dismisses Clinton move on Helms-Burton.

text.p: Cuba dismissed on Friday U.S. President Bill Clinton's move to delay implementation of a law that would allow U.S. citizens to sue some foreign companies doing business on the communist-ruled island.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Miguel Alfonso said the Helms-Burton law, one part of whose implementation was suspended again for six months on Friday by Clinton, remained unchanged.

"In the end, it's just more of the same, the only thing that happens is that the rest of the world is given its full sovereignty for six months and then there will be another period of uncertainty," he told reporters.
"It's a negotiating weapon so that other countries adapt their policies to those of the United States," Alfonso added.

Clinton ordered a further six-month suspension of Title Three of Helms-Burton, having first suspended implementation last July. He said he would continue to suspend the provision as long as U.S. allies continued a stepped-up effort to promote democracy and human rights in Cuba.
Title Three would allow U.S. citizens to sue foreign companies doing business with property nationalized after Fidel Castro's 1959 revolution.
Alfonso said the rest of the law had not been suspended.

"Titles One and Two, which are clearly interfering in nature, and Title Four, which allows company executives to be punished, remain in place," Alfonso said. "It's obvious that the extra-territorial nature of the law still stands."

Titles One and Two demanded radical political change in Cuba, while Title Four allowed the United States to bar from entry executives of foreign firms deemed to be doing business on expropriated property.
This last provision was used against executives from a Canadian mining firm and a Mexican telecommunications company that invested in Cuba.

Helms-Burton, enacted in March, enraged Europeans, Canadians and Mexicans who argued the United States was trying to impose its anti-Cuba trade sanctions on them. A number of countries have moved to enact laws to counter Helms-Burton and filed trade complaints with the World Trade Organization.
Cuba was similarly cool last July when Clinton first suspended implementation of Title Three.

Asked about how Cuba might view a similar move this month, parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon said in a state television interview Dec. 31 that further suspension would not help. The only real solution to Helms-Burton was to dump it in the rubbish bin, he said.

Cuba, slowly emerging from economic crisis triggered by the collapse of its one-time economic ally the former Soviet Union, has said foreign investors have not left the island and new investors have not stopped coming as a result of the law, approved by Clinton after Havana shot down two small private U.S. planes last February.
But foreign diplomats in Havana say the law is bound to delay investment and is also hurting the island's ability to secure credits.
